5.38.m: Sūta said: / Having heard this narrative, the noble-minded Vātsyāyana / experienced supreme joy and said to the lord of serpents:
Vātsyāyana said: / “There is no satiation for me as I listen to the story, O lord of serpents, / of Raghunātha, who dispels the distress of his devotees and creates renown.
Blessed is the supreme sage named Āraṇyaka, a knower of the Vedas, / who, having gazed upon Raghunātha, abandoned his perishable body!
Where did the king’s horse go after that? By whom was it restrained? / How did the glory of the Lord of Ramā arise there, O lord of serpents?
Tell me all in truth, since you are omniscient, / bearing the form of the supporter of the earth, possessing his direct form.”
Vyāsa said: / Having heard this speech, with a joyful inner self, / he spoke the story of Rāma’s deeds, an arising of tales of his various virtues.
Śeṣa said: / “Well do you ask, O Brahmin sage, again and again about the virtues of Raghunātha, / treating what was heard as if unheard, bearing an eager craving for them.
Then the horse set forth, surrounded by many soldiers, / along the charming bank of the Revā, frequented by hosts of sages.
Then all the soldiers, skilled in battle, advanced wherever the horse went, / watching its path in every direction.
Then the steed, bearing a golden plate on its forehead and with its limbs worshipped, / entered a pool in the Revā that contained fathomless water.
Then that excellent horse of Rāmacandra sank into the water; / at that time all the great heroes there were struck with astonishment.
They said among themselves: “How shall we recover the horse? / Who here will enter into the water to bring back that magnificent steed?”
While they were anxiously taking counsel with one another, / just then the lord of Raghu's line arrived along with hundreds of heroes.
Seeing all of them dejected, the crest-jewel of heroes, known as Śatrughna, / asked in a voice deep as a thundercloud:
"Why are all of you standing gathered today at the water? / Where is the horse of the lord of the Raghus, adorned with the golden plate?
Has it sunk in the water, or has it been seized by some proud man? / Tell me that quickly! Why are you bewildered?"
Śeṣa said: / Having heard these words of the king, the best of the Raghus, / those heroes reported everything to the crest-jewel of heroes.
The men said: / "O master, we do not know. It was in the water for a moment, / and then it sank down; your handsome horse did not emerge from there.
You yourself, having gone there, bring back that horse with speed! / O wise one, we should go there along with you."
Having heard those words of the soldiers, the scion of Raghu / felt sorrow upon seeing the people preparing to cross the water.
He said to the chief minister: "What must be done after this? / Speak of that: how will the retrieval of the horse take place?
Which heroes should be dispatched there to search for the horse in the water? / Or who will bring back the horse, and by what means? Tell that!"
Having heard the words of the king, Sumati, the best of ministers, / addressed Śatrughna at the proper time, as if bringing him joy:
"O illustrious master of wondrous deeds, you possess the power / to travel clearly to Pātāla from the midst of the water here.
Moreover, the great-souled Puṣkala also has the power, / and so does Hanūmat, who is devoted to the service of Rāma's feet.
Therefore, the three of you go and surely bring back the horse, / so that the horse sacrifice of the wise lord of the Raghus may proceed."
Śeṣa said: / Having heard these words, Śatrughna, the slayer of enemy heroes, / entered beneath the waters himself, accompanied by Hanumat and Puṣkala.
As soon as he entered the water, a city appeared, / an immeasurable fortified city, rich with the beauty of many gardens.
There he saw the horse of Rāma, adorned with the golden plate, / tied to a golden pillar inlaid with rubies.
Excellent women bearing captivating beauty / were attending upon a single lovely woman who sat comfortably upon a couch.
Seeing them, all those women said to their mistress: / "These men are youthful in age, their bodies plump with flesh.
They will become the great and excellent reward for your meal; / sweet is the blood of these men whose life-spans have run out!"
Hearing these words of her servants, the faultless, excellent woman / laughed slightly, making her face dance with her eyebrows.
Meanwhile, the three arrived, resplendent with the splendor of their armor, / wearing helmets, endowed with valor and prowess.
Seeing those women there endowed with the splendor of beauty, / they said in wonder, O twice-born: "What great sight is seen here?"
All those great-souled men then paid homage to the celestial women, / their pairs of feet illuminated by the radiance of the crest-jewels.
She, the proud lady, the best of all, asked those men: / "Who are you that have arrived here, bearing bows, as mortals?
My place is inaccessible even to all the gods, great and bewitching; / for anyone who reaches here, there is indeed no return anywhere.
To which king does this horse belong, fanned with chowries / and rich in beauty with its golden plate? Let them speak before me!"
Śeṣa said: / Having heard her words, coupled with enchanting conduct, / Hanūmān, devoid of fear, answered her as if laughing:
"We are indeed the servants of the king who is the crest-gem of the three worlds, / to whom, the crest-jewel of all the gods, the three worlds bow.
Know him to be Rāmabhadra, the initiator of the horse sacrifice! / Release our horse! Why has it been tied up, O excellent lady?
We are skilled in all mystical weapons and knowledgeable in all arms and missiles; / we will take the horse by force after slaying those who obstruct it!"
Having heard these words of the monkey, the noble woman / standing in the cave, skilled in speech, smilingly replied:
"No one is able to release this horse brought by me, / even in ten thousand years with crores of sharp arrows of blazing crests.
However, being a female servant performing service at Rāma's lotus feet, / I will not seize that horse of the wise king of kings.
A great disrespect was committed by me in leading away the fine horse; / may Rāmabhadra forgive that, he who is the refuge, affectionate to his devotees!
You men are distressed on account of the horse of that protector; / ask for a boon unobtainable even by the gods, O excellent ones,
so that the supreme person may forgive this very terrible offense of mine! / Casting away all hesitation, choose an excellent boon!"

Hearing her supreme words, Hanūmān said to her: / "By the grace of the lord of the Raghus, everything of ours is prosperous.

"Even so, I ask for one supreme boon: / grant that which is desired by my mind."
In birth after birth, let the leader of the Raghus be our lord, / and may we be the performers of his deeds and his attendants!"
Hearing these words of the monkey, the lady then / spoke sweet words, laughing, honoured for their virtue:
"That which you have requested, difficult to obtain even by all the gods, / will come to pass, without a doubt, O servants of that lord of the Raghus!
Moreover, I, who committed an insult, shall give you one boon / for the satisfaction of the lord of the Raghus, so that my word may prove true:
Ahead, King Vīramaṇi, accompanied by great heroes, / guarded by Śiva, will seize your horse.
For conquering him, receive my great missile, O ones of very great might! / In single combat on chariots, that great man must be fought by you, Śatrughna.
When, however, you discharge this missile in battle, / purified by it, he will directly realize the true nature of Rāma.
Knowing that, he will give up the horse and fall at [his] feet; / therefore, accept that missile of mine which tears through enemies!"
Hearing that, the brother of the lord of the Raghus took the missile; / facing north, with a purified body, [he received] the wondrous gift given by the yoginī.
Obtaining that missile, he of great splendor became an afflicter of enemies, / difficult to overcome, hard to resist, a veritable goad to the elephant of his foes.
Bowing to her, Śatrughna, the best of the Rāghavas, taking the excellent horse, / went out from that water to the pleasant bank of the Revā.
Seeing him, all the soldiers, their limbs thrilled with delight, filled with joy, / praising him with 'Well done, well done!', asked about the emergence of the horse.
Hanūmān related the great return of the horse / and the attainment of the boon from her; hearing it, they too were filled with joy.

5.39.m: Śeṣa said: / As the mṛdaṅgas resounded and the sounds of the vīṇās [arose] on all sides, / the horse was released from there toward Devapura, built by the gods.
Where, with their crystal wall constructions, the mansions of mortals / laugh at the spotless Vindhya mountain inhabited by serpents;
Where houses of silver are seen, surpassing even nature, / fitted with marvelous gems and possessing gates adorned with various rubies;
Where charming, lotus-like women in house after house / captivate the minds of men with their lotus faces and gentle glances;
Where ruby gems set into the fine floors of every house / seem, O brāhmaṇa, as if competing with their lower lips;
Where pleasure hills made of sapphires at every dwelling / cause the crested peacocks to mistake them for rainclouds;
Where swans kept in the crystal houses of mortals / feel no fear of clouds, nor do they remember Lake Mānasa;
Where, in that abode of Śiva, darkness is perpetually dispelled by moonlight, / so that among men there is no distinction between the light and dark fortnights.
There King Vīramaṇi, foremost among the righteous, / rules over a vast kingdom endowed with all pleasures.
His mighty son, a great hero named Rukmāṅgada, / went into the forest to play accompanied by lovely-bodied women.
The tinkling of their anklets and the sound of their bracelets / bewitched the mind of the god of love himself; what need to speak of any other, sir?
He went to a very great forest filled with flowering trees, / made into a dwelling place by Sadāśiva, splendid in all six seasons;
Where campaka trees, abundantly adorned with blooming buds / and seen on every side, torment lovers with the pain of desire;
Where mango trees are bent low with fruits and myriad blossoms, / along with nāga and punnāga trees, sāl trees, palms, and tamālas;
Where the cooing of cuckoos reaches the ear, / and fine jasmine flowers are ever awakened from sleep by the humming of bees;
Which is radiant with clusters of pomegranate trees mixed with karṇikāras, / ketakīs, and lines of various other forest trees.

Into that forest, his mind full of delight, singing softly with a sweet voice out of a desire for pleasure, / surrounded on all sides by women with rising breasts, his body a storehouse of beauty, he entered without fear.
Some pleased that handsome prince with their knowledge of dance, / some with their arts of singing, and some with clever, well-timed speech.
Other impassioned women delighted him with signals of their eyebrows, / and the women made him glad with skillful embraces.
Gathering flowers with them, he adorned those women; / praising them with tender words, he sported like Kāma incarnate.

While the wise king of kings was occupied in this way, / that exceedingly handsome horse arrived at that forest region.

...that [horse] whose single forehead region was adorned with a golden plaque, / whose body was yellowed with saffron paste resembling the Ganges...

with a gait that surpassed the speed of the wind— / seeing that steed whose body was an abode of supreme wonder,

...reddish-brown in color like the center of a lotus, / the striking lustre of whose coppery lower lips defeated coral, spoke to their husband:
with faces radiant with smiles that revealed rows of teeth, / and whose eyes resembled the bewitching arrows of Kāma, said to their lord:

The women said:
“Beloved, what great horse is this, adorned with a single gold plate? / Whose magnificent steed is it? Seize it by your own might!”

Śeṣa said:
Hearing the words spoken by them, his eyes playful and charming, / he playfully seized the horse with one lotus hand.
Having read the gold plate inscribed with clear letters, / he laughed in the midst of the women and spoke once more.

Rukmāṅgada said:
“On earth there is none equal to my father in valor and majesty; / how then can King Rāma display such arrogance toward him?
He whom Rudra, wielder of the Pināka, protects at all times, / and before whom gods, Dānavas, and Yakṣas bow with jeweled crests—
let my father of great power perform a horse sacrifice instead! / Let this horse go to the stable, and let my warriors tie it fast.”
Having heard these words, those charming women / became joyous-faced and embraced their beloved.
Taking the horse, the great son of King Vīramaṇi, / accompanied by his wives, entered the city with tremendous enthusiasm.
Amid the loud striking of mṛdaṅga drums all around, / eulogized by bards, he proceeded to his father's grand palace.
He told him that the horse of the lord of the Raghus had been seized— / that wondrous horse released for the horse sacrifice, wandering at will,
and protected by the slayer of enemies who was joined by a mighty army. / Hearing his words, the great king Vīramaṇi,
though very wise, did not overly praise that deed; / taking it and returning seemed to him like the conduct of a thief.
He reported it to his son-in-law, Śiva of wondrous deeds, / who bears a woman on half his body, whose body is adorned with serpents, and who wears the moon.
The great king Vīramaṇi consulted with him / about this rash deed committed by his son, which is blameworthy in the opinion of the wise.

Śiva said:
“O King, a most astonishing deed has been performed by your son, / who seized the great steed of the wise Rāmacandra!
Today a great battle will take place, bewitching gods and asuras, / against the great king Śatrughna, who alone protects tens of millions of warriors.
He whom I hold in my heart and constantly utter with my tongue— / your young son has stolen the sacrificial horse of that very Rāma.
Yet a great gain will indeed come from this in battle: / we shall behold Rāma’s lotus feet, which are served by me.
A great effort must be made here in protecting the horse; / for they will take the horse by force even though it is protected by me.
Therefore, O great king, bow humbly and offer this horse / along with your kingdom; feed it well, and then gaze upon his pair of feet.”
Having heard these words of Śiva, that best of kings / spoke to him, whose pair of lotus feet is worshipped by the lord of the gods and others:

Vīramaṇi said:
“This is the duty of kṣatriyas: the protection of their own prowess. / Yet he is preparing to overcome that through this sacrifice called the horse sacrifice.
Therefore one’s own prowess must be protected by any proud man by whatever means, / even by sacrificing his body, after doing all that lies within his power.
All this was done by my son because the horse has been captured; / O Lord, act as is suitable to the occasion toward the angered King Rāma.
This cannot be an action worthy of being done by kṣatriyas— / that one should suddenly bow down at the feet of an enemy, overwhelmed with fear.
Enemies laugh at such a one, thinking: ‘This vile king is a coward, / a petty, low person like a vulgar man, who has bowed down agitated by fear!’
Therefore, when battle is at hand, after considering what is proper / and what ought to be done, you must indeed protect your devotee.”

Śeṣa said:
Hearing this speech, the moon-crested god replied, / laughing, with a voice deep as a thundercloud that captivated the mind:
“Even if the thirty-three crores of gods should come forth, / still, who could take the horse from you while I protect it?
If Rāma himself comes and shows himself, / then I shall bow down to his exceedingly tender feet.
One should never fight with one's master; that is called a great impropriety. / The other warriors are like blades of grass, completely unable to accomplish anything.”
"Therefore fight, O king of kings, while I stand well as your protector. / Who can seize the horse by force, even if the three worlds unite?"
Śeṣa said: / Having heard these supreme words of the Moon-crested God, the king / rejoiced greatly in his mind, eager for the act of battle.

5.40.m: Śeṣa said: / The scouts of the great king, endowed with great strength, / arrived searching for that horse of King Rāma.
"Where is that horse? By whom has it been taken? Or why is it not to be seen? / Who is this very foolish person who would go to the city of Yama after stealing the horse?"
While the scouts of Raghu's descendant were searching along his trail, / just then the great king arrived, surrounded by a mighty army.
He questioned all the servants: "Where is my horse now? / Why is the horse adorned with the gold plate not seen?"
Having heard those words of his, the attendants following the horse / said: "O master, the steed, swift as thought, [has been captured] in the forest by someone!"
carried off; therefore it is not seen by us, skilled though we are in tracking. / Therefore, an effort must be made here, O Lord, toward recovering the horse."
Hearing their words, King Śatrughna questioned Sumati— / he who caused the destruction of enemies, endowed with an enchanting form.
Śatrughna said: / "Who is the king that lives here? How was the encounter with the horse? / How great is the strength of that king by whom my horse has been carried off today?"
Sumati said: / "O King, this is indeed Devapura, built by God himself, / impassable as Kailāsa to closely united hosts of enemies.
In it King Vīramaṇi, a mighty hero endowed with prowess, / rules the kingdom according to dharma, protected by Śiva.
He who is the author of dissolution abides here, subjugated by devotion— / the Moon-crested God, always showing partiality toward his own devotee.
Therefore, if it has been seized, a great battle will take place here. / Alert, let them indeed protect the camp."
Hearing this, that Śatrughna, crest-jewel of all kings, / having formed a battle array of his army, stood there, illustrious in fame.
Then, as he sat at ease taking counsel with his good minister, / that divine sage arrived, eager for battle.
Seeing that sage, a treasure-house of austerities, arrived, / Śatrughna stood up, seated him on a seat, and offered the honey-mixture.
And pleasing with his speech Nārada, the best of sages, who was gratified by the welcome, / he, skilled in eloquence, spoke:
Śatrughna said: / "Where is my horse, O brahmin? Tell me, O noble-minded one! / Its path is not perceived by my skilled servants.
Declare by which proud kṣatriya it was carried off! / How will the recovery of the horse come about here, O rich in austerity?"
Having heard these words of Śatrughna, Nārada, / sounding his vīṇā and singing repeatedly the story of Rāma, spoke:
Nārada said: / "This is Devapura, O King; the great Vīramaṇi is its king. / By his son staying in the forest your royal steed has been seized.
There a great and exceedingly terrible battle will happen for you today; / in it heroes endowed with might and valor will fall.
Therefore, you must remain here with great effort, O mighty one; / construct an array formation impenetrable to enemy warriors!
Victory will be yours, O King, with difficulty, over this best of kings; / who indeed could defeat Rāma in the entire world?"
Having spoken thus, the brāhmaṇa vanished and then took his stand in the sky, / wishing to behold the exceedingly fierce battle, like that between gods and dānavas.
Śeṣa said: / Then King Vīramaṇi, crest-jewel of all heroes, / in order to sound a loud drum in the middle of his own city,
summoned his commander-in-chief, a champion against enemies, lofty in stature, / and spoke quickly in a voice deep as a thundercloud:
Vīramaṇi said: / "O commander, issue the proclamation of the drum in my splendid city: / 'Hearing it, well-equipped, let them march against Śatrughna!'"
Having heard these words, he then caused King Vīramaṇi's / kettle-drum to resound with a mighty roar.
"In every house and on every road the sound of the drum is heard: / 'Let all heroes residing in the royal city march against Śatrughna!
Those proud warriors who transgress the command of the king, / whether sons or brothers, shall be put to death by royal order!
Let the heroes hear again the sound when the drum is struck; / having heard it, let what is to be done be performed quickly, with no delay!'"
their bodies adorned with golden armor, / the store of their hearts delighted by the great festival of war.
Some went wearing splendid helmets on their heads, / richly adorned with armor, splendid as hundreds of millions [of suns].
By chariot with a pair of horses, gleaming with jewels and gold, / they went at the king's command toward the monarch's palace, intoxicated with zeal.
Some on rutting elephants, others on splendid horses, / all fulfilling the king's command, went to the ruler's residence.
Adorned with pure gold armor and a helmet, / Rukmāṅgada too stood in his own chariot that was swift as thought.
His younger brother, Śubhāṅgada, wearing on his body an excellent armor / made of great jewels, set out for the festival of battle.
The king's brother, Vīrasiṃha, skilled in all weapons and missiles, / went there by the king's order, obeying the command of the monarch.
The son-in-law of that king, known as Balamitra, / fully equipped, armored, and sword-bearing, went to the king's palace.
The commander Ripuvāra also, having made ready / that fourfold army, then announced it, great as he was, to the king.
Then King Vīramaṇi mounted an excellent chariot / filled with all weapons and missiles, its high wheels fashioned of gems.
Then, in that ocean of warriors, the blast of conches was heard on every side, / as if urging timid heroes on in the combat.
Drums were struck on all sides, beaten by skilled drummers, / where his army divisions stood ready, having set out for battle.
All, having received blessings, adorned with all ornaments, / fully supplied with all weapons and missiles, went to the field of battle.
And the mountain caves were filled with the roar of drums and conches; / did that sound go, as it were, to summon those who dwell in heaven?
While that tumult was taking place, the great king Vīramaṇi, / filled with the enthusiasm of battle, went to the battle ground.
Having arrived, he stood there, densely filled with chariots and foot soldiers, / as if an ocean had come to flood men from that place.
Seeing that army arrived, raised to a tumult / by car-warriors skilled in weapons, the king said to Sumati:
Śatrughna said: / "The mighty Vīramaṇi, captor of my horse, has arrived / with a great fourfold army to fight me again.
How should the battle be fought? Who are those formidable in strength who will fight? / Point out all those warriors to me, so that the desired victory may be attained."

Sumati said:
"O Lord, this great king, surrounded by a mighty army,
has arrived for battle, endowed with devotion to Śiva.

Now let the heroic Puṣkala, who knows supreme missiles, fight,
as well as other warriors skilled in battle, headed by Nīla and Ratna.
"You must fight with Śiva, O sinless one, or with the king; / he of great strength and prowess must be conquered in single combat."

By this method, O king, your victory will come to pass here;
afterwards, do whatever pleases you, O lord of great intellect!"

Śeṣa said:
Having heard this speech, Śatrughna, slayer of enemy warriors,
resolved upon battle and then commanded his fine warriors:

"Along with all the armies, for battle with the kings skilled in weapons,
effort must be made again so that my victory will come swiftly!"

Having heard this, those skilled in war, for the sake of Rāghava's victory,
filled with great zeal, went forth to fight with their soldiers.

5.41.m:
Śeṣa said:
Well-equipped for battle, Śatrughna's mighty men,
endowed with valor, advanced into the midst of Vīramaṇi's army.

Releasing arrows, piercing many soldiers,
those men bearing bows were seen standing within the battle.

Many were slain there: elephants and chariots adorned with gems,
and shattered ones along with their horses were seen in the field of battle.

Hearing that slaughter had been wrought upon them, the mighty Rukmāṅgada,
standing in his gem-studded chariot, advanced with his soldiers to fight.

Placing arrows on his bow, holding inexhaustible quivers,
with the corners of his eyes blood-red, terrifying, filled with great fury,

making heroes tremble by thousands with his numerous arrows,
causing lamentation, the mighty Rukmāṅgada advanced.

The mighty prince challenged Śatrughna's [son] Puṣkala,
[son of] Bhāratī, who was his equal in strength, fame, and splendor.

Rukmāṅgada said:
"Come forth, you whose deeds are heroic, of great strength and valor,
to fight with me, a radiant prince possessing mighty power!

What is the use of other men being terrified and slain by the millions, O hero?
Engage in a great fight with me and achieve victory!"
To him who had spoken thus, the mighty Puṣkala, laughing heartily, swiftly / struck right in the middle of his broad chest with sharp-jointed [arrows].

Not enduring that, the prince placed arrows on his great bow
and struck the hero Puṣkala with ten shafts in his chest.

Both eager for battle, both desiring victory,
they shone in battle like Kumāra and Tāraka.

Fixing ten exceedingly sharp arrows upon his bow,
the heroic Puṣkala deprived the prince of his chariot.

With four he felled the four horses, with two the charioteer,
with one his flag, and with two the two chariot-guards.

With one, the swift warrior pierced the prince in the heart;
seeing that wondrous feat, all the heroes were delighted.

With his bow severed, chariotless, his horses and charioteer slain,
he became exceedingly enraged and mounted another chariot.

Standing in that excellent chariot adorned with the best of horses,
taking up a mighty, very firm bow, strung with a cord,

Rukmāṅgada addressed this speech to the heroic Puṣkala:
"Having displayed great valor, where will you go, O scorcher of foes?

Behold today my prowess, wrought by my strength!
Stand firm with effort, O hero; I shall cast your chariot into the sky!"
Having spoken thus, he placed an exceedingly terrible arrow upon his bow; / then, having consecrated a whirling missile, [he hurled it] at the chariot of Puṣkala's son.

he released the sharp arrow adorned with golden feathers;
by that arrow, his chariot was carried a full yojana.

Held back with difficulty by his charioteer, the chariot whirled upon the earth;
having regained his place with difficulty, Puṣkala, knower of supreme missiles,

bearing an arrow on his bow, spoke these words to him:
"Attain heaven, O best of heroes, served by all the gods!

Those like you are not fit for the earth, O best of kings,
but fit for the assembly of Śatakratu; therefore, go to the abode of the gods!"
Having spoken thus, he released a mighty weapon that sent [its target] into the sky; / by that arrow, he along with his chariot flew upwards into the air.

Passing beyond all the worlds, he reached the orb of the sun;
by its flame his chariot was burned, along with his horses and charioteer.

With his body mostly scorched by its rays, deeply distressed,
he fell down, holding in his heart the Crescent-Crested God who relieves affliction.

Fallen there upon the ground, his body scorched by the rays,
plunged into extreme agony, he swooned on the battlefield.

When that prince had fallen to the ground in a swoon,
there was a great cry of lamentation at the forefront of the battle.

Those enemies headed by Puṣkala obtained the fortune of victory;
the enemy horse-guards became intent on flight.

Then, seeing the swoon of his son, King Vīramaṇi,
filled with anger, advanced toward Puṣkala, who stood in the midst of battle.

Then this earth shook, along with its excellent mountains and forests;
the heroes were filled with joy, while the cowards were afflicted with fear.

Holding a great bow and two inexhaustible quivers,
breathing heavily in wrath, he challenged his enemy.

5.42.m:
Śeṣa said:
Seeing that king challenging Puṣkala in the ocean of the great army,
Hanūmān, lord of monkeys, also rushed toward him.

Raising his tail, his body enormous, / spreading a roar like the rumbling of a raincloud...

[passing by] the foremost heroes standing in the fight, the monkey-lord
went toward that best of kings, Vīramaṇi.

Seeing that Hanūmān approaching, the formidable Puṣkala
gazed at him with eyes very red with anger toward the foe.

Puṣkala, knower of supreme missiles, addressed Hanūmān
with a voice deep as a thundercloud, making the battleground resound:

Puṣkala said:
"Why have you come to fight in battle, O great monkey?
How much is this little strength of King Vīramaṇi?

Where all the three worlds have assembled in front,
there do you wish to go to fight in sport or not?

Who is this King Vīramaṇi? How trifling is his strength!
Your coming here in such fierce fury is not fitting, O hero.

By the glance of Raghunātha's grace, crossing over what is impassable,
I shall finish him in an instant, O lord of monkeys; do not set your mind on the battle!

By you the ocean of rakṣasas was crossed by the power of Rāma's grace;
likewise, meditating well on Rāma, I shall cross over what is impassable.

Whoever, facing what is impassable, remember Raghunātha,
their ocean of grief will dry up, of this there is no doubt.

Therefore go to the side of Śatrughna, O mighty hero!
Having conquered King Vīramaṇi in an instant, I am coming!"
Śeṣa said: / Having heard these steadfast words spoken by Puṣkala, / the slayer of enemy heroes spoke once again to Puṣkala.
Hanumān said: / “My son, do not act rashly against King Vīramaṇi. / He is generous and a granter of refuge, endowed with might and valor.
You are a boy, while the king is an elder, the foremost knower of all weapons and missiles. / Many heroes shining with great valor have been conquered by him in battle.
Know that Sadāśiva is at his side as his protector, / Sthāṇu, united with Umā, brought under his power through devotion and dwelling in this city.
Therefore, Puṣkala, I myself will fight with this king. / You, conquer other heroes and win abundant renown.”
Puṣkala said: / “Śiva was brought under control through devotion and established by him in his city; / but Maheśvara does not reside directly within that [king's] heart.
That very Sadāśiva, having worshiped whom he reached the supreme station, / is Rāma, who never departs anywhere, abandoning my heart.
Where Rāma is, there is the entire universe, both motionless and moving. / Therefore, I will conquer King Vīramaṇi in battle.
Go, O monkey, to fight in battle with the other proud, foremost kings / headed by Vīrasiṃha; do not worry about me, O lord.”
Having heard this speech cherished by the wise, / Hanūmān went into battle to fight Vīrasiṃha, the king's younger brother.
Lakṣmīnidhi engaged in a chariot duel with his son, / the celebrated Śubhāṅgada, an expert in great weapons and missiles.
With Balamitra, Sumada, exalted by the power of his own majesty / and armed with weapons, advanced into the battle to fight, that prince.
Seeing that king issuing a challenge to single chariot combat, Puṣkala, skilled in warfare, / mounted upon his gold-inlaid chariot, went straight toward him.
Seeing that Puṣkala, skilled in battle, had approached, / the king, addressed with pleasant words, spoke in the midst of the fight with a fearless voice.
Vīramaṇi said: / “Boy, do not approach me, enraged and fiercely wrathful in battle! / Go, to save your life; do not fight with me!
Kings like me take pity on boys such as you, / and they never strike them. Therefore, depart from the battle!
As long as I have not beheld you with my eyes, I was agitated; / now, my mind has no desire to strike you.
As for your having pierced my son with arrows and rendered him unconscious, / all of that has been forgiven by me today, because of your childish understanding, great as it was.”
Having heard these words, Puṣkala said to him: / Puṣkala said: / "I am a boy; you are very old, skilled in all weapons and missiles."
Yet this is the conviction of kṣatriyas: those endowed with superior strength / are the truly aged, O foremost of kings, not those who have merely advanced in years.
Your son, proud of his valor and might, was struck down unconscious by me. / Now I will fell you with weapons in the contest of war.
Therefore, O king, take your stand with effort at the head of the battle! / No one, even standing in Indra's rank, can conquer me, a devotee of Rāma.”
Hearing this spoken by Puṣkala, the leader of kings / laughed on looking at the boy, and then became angry once again.
Seeing him enraged, Bharata's furious son / struck the king in the chest with twenty sharp arrows.
Seeing those arrows released by him approaching, the king, / exceedingly enraged, cut them into many pieces with sharp arrows.
Seeing the cutting of his arrows, the son of Bharata, slayer of enemy heroes, / grew intensely angry in his heart, and with three arrows,
that king's son named Puṣkala pierced [him] in the forehead. / Lodged there, they shone—were they the three peaks of Trikūṭa?

Afflicted by those arrows, the king, filled with great fury, / struck heroic Puṣkala in the chest with nine arrows. / By those calf-toothed shafts, much blood of the son of Rāma's younger brother was drunk;
they remained fixed in his body like enraged venomous serpents. / Falling into supreme anger, Puṣkala once again
swiftly pierced the ruler of the earth with a hundred sharp-jointed arrows. / By those arrows, his armor was shattered, and his diadem along with his helmet,
his chariot, and his great strung bow were severed by the overflow of wrath. / Drenched in blood, his body pierced by arrows,
he mounted another chariot and advanced toward Bharata's son: / “Blessed are you, O hero, bee at the lotus feet of Rāma!
A great deed was done by you today, in that I was deprived of my chariot. / Protect your life, O hero, while I fight now!
Your life will not be easily kept, with me standing before you in the form of Death!” / Having spoken thus, the master of weapons struck him with countless arrows.
On the earth and in every direction, nothing was seen there except his arrows. / Many thousands of elephants were pierced, and horses on all sides;
chariots along with their charioteers were cut, shattered, and cleaved in two by him. / A river with torrents of blood flowed forth there on the battlefield,
where furious elephants appeared like mountain peaks, / and hair from the heads of creatures looked like moss again and again.
Severed hands of many heroes, splendid with rings / and smeared with sandal paste and other unguents, appeared there like serpents.
The heads of the foremost warriors bore the likeness of tortoises, / and the flesh of great heroes formed the mud there.
While such a tumult was taking place, hundreds of yoginīs in the battle / drank the blood of creatures fallen in the fight from vessels.
Filled with joy and curiosity, they devoured flesh; / having drunk the blood there and eaten the flesh, maddened with frenzy,
they danced, laughed aloud, and sang loudly on the field of slaughter. / Piśācas on that battlefield, taking in both hands
the heads of creatures, their limbs intoxicated, set about beating them like cymbals. / Jackals there, having devoured the great flesh
of those fallen on the battleground, howled in frenzy, inspiring terror in cowards. / Stricken with fear, the cowards entered the hollows of elephants,
and were devoured by the yoginīs—for the wicked have no refuge anywhere! / Observing this destruction of his own army, that foremost of chariot-warriors,
Puṣkala, also wrought slaughter in the circle of battle: / the heads of elephants were split open, and pearls spilled forth;
that river filled with hair appeared like the Tāmraparṇī. / The arrows shot by Puṣkala, striking the limbs of men, / severed the lives of even the heroes on all sides.
All their limbs drenched in blood, all with their own bodies mutilated, / the fine warriors on the field of slaughter appeared like kiṃśuka trees.
At that moment, enraged, having challenged the king, / [Puṣkala], overwhelmed by a flood of fury, struck him with many arrows.
With his limbs pierced by the penetration of those arrows and his armor shattered, the king, / considering him to possess great might, struck back with ten million arrows.
Discharged through his armor by those arrows, abundant blood flowed forth; / his handsome body became the object of a cage of arrows.
Standing within that cage of arrows, his mind overwhelmed, / that son of Bharata was unable either to draw or to fit his shafts.
Remembering Rāma and grasping his great, strong bow strung in his hand, / he discharged sharp arrows that repulsed the host of his foes.
Dispersing that cage of arrows with those shafts, O best of sages, / he blew his conch shell in battle and, freed of fear, addressed the king:
Puṣkala said: / 'A great deed was done by you, O hero, when you made me / fall into your cage of arrows, distressing formidable warriors.
Because of your old age, you are venerable to me right now on the field of battle. / Today, O King, crest-jewel of heroes, behold my great prowess!
If I do not make you swoon with three arrows, O hero, / then hear a solemn vow that confounds all warriors:
Even after reaching the Gaṅgā, the great sinner, engaging in foolish actions, / who censures that remover of sins and does not bathe in her—
let his sin be mine alone, O hero, if on the battlefield / I do not fell you in a swoon! Ready yourself, O lord of the earth!'
Having heard these words of Puṣkala, the best of kings / grew furious, deeply perturbed, and fitted sharp arrows to his bow.
Piercing the chest of that great son of Bharata, those arrows went forth / and fell down upon the earth, just like those who turn away from devotion to Rāma.
Then [Puṣkala] released a sharp arrow, blazing like fire, at him, / aiming at his broad chest, which was wide as a door-panel.
That arrow, split in two by an arrow of the king, / fell down into the chariot, glowing like the disc of the sun.
Then, having dedicated his merit, he placed another arrow born of devotion to his mother; / but [Vīramaṇi] cut down that one as well with a great [arrow].
Distressed at heart, pondering what was to be done, / and remembering Rāma, the dispeller of his distress, in his heart, that master of supreme missiles released [another].
That arrow, resembling a venomous serpent and blazing with radiance like the sun, / struck his chest and threw him into a swoon.
Then a great cry of grief arose from all sides, and everyone turned to flight; / the king having fallen unconscious, Puṣkala attained victory.

5.43.m: Śeṣa said: / Approaching Vīrasiṃha, Hanūmān spoke these words: / 'Halt! Where will you flee, O hero? In an instant I shall conquer you here!'
Hearing these great words of the monkey spoken thus, / [Vīrasiṃha], consumed by a surge of wrath, twanged his bow that roared like a cloud;
sounding it, he shone in battle, discharging terrible, sharp arrows, / looking enchanting like a rain-cloud pouring down a torrent of water in the month of Āṣāḍha.
Seeing those sharp arrows deeply penetrating his body, / Hanūmān, the son of Añjanā, became exceedingly enraged in his heart.
With his fist, which possessed the hardness of a thunderbolt, he struck him in the chest; / struck by that fist, the hero fell onto the surface of the earth.
Seeing his uncle unconscious, that auspiciously adorned Aṅgada, / and Rukmāṅgada too, cast off his faint and went to the battlefield.
Raining arrows like two thunderous clouds / and causing terrible slaughter, they rushed toward the monkey.
Seeing those two heroes advancing in battle, the lord of monkeys / entwined them, along with their chariots and bows, with his tail,
and dashed them against the ground. Instantly both swooned; / with their bodies stained with blood, they became motionless.
Balamitra, having fought for a long time with great arrogance, / was indeed made to swoon by [Hanūmān's] arrows with very sharp joints.
Brought in an instant by Puṣkala into a swoon devoid of consciousness, / victory was attained by the army of Śatrughna that afflicted enemy warriors.
At that moment, Śiva, mounted on his excellent chariot / and bending his divine bow, charged toward those warriors.
The great [lord], bearing the crescent moon nestled within his matted hair, / wearing serpent ornaments that touched his mind, held the Ājagava bow.
Seeing his people fallen unconscious, Maheśvara, the destroyer of his devotees' affliction, / advanced with great armies to fight these warriors of Śatrughna.
Surrounded by his troops and retinue, making the surface of the earth tremble, / he came to protect his devotees, just as he once marched against Tripura.
Bearing eyes exceedingly red with rage, bringing about universal dissolution, / the wielder of the Pināka, praised by the gods, gazed upon the esteemed warriors.
Seeing that Maheśāna had arrived, the mighty younger brother of Rāma / advanced into battle to fight the crest-jewel of all the gods.
Then, seeing Śatrughna approach, Rudra, the bearer of the Pināka, / overcome with deep anger, holding his strung bow, spoke:
'A grave deed was committed by Puṣkala, the worshipper of Rāma's feet, / who, having struck down my devotee in battle, has come to the battleground!
Where is that great hero now, Puṣkala, the master of supreme missiles? / By slaying him in battle, that tormentor of my devotee, I shall find relief!'
Śeṣa said: / Having spoken thus, he dispatched Vīrabhadra against Puṣkala: / 'Go you to fight Puṣkala in battle, that harasser of my servant!'
He dispatched Nandin against the mighty Hanūmān, / the fierce Kuśadhvaja against Bhṛṅgin, and Subāhuka;
against Sumada he directed his own attendant named Caṇḍa. / Then Puṣkala, seeing the great attendant Vīrabhadra approaching,
sent by great Rudra, the noble-minded one advanced to fight. / Puṣkala struck him with five arrows in the encounter.
His limbs pierced by those arrows, [Vīrabhadra] hurled his trident; / but the mighty [Puṣkala] shattered that trident in an instant and roared aloud.
Seeing his own trident broken, that mighty follower of Rudra / swiftly struck the son of Bharata on the head with his skull-topped staff, O twice-born one.
Struck by the skull-topped staff, that formidable warrior swooned for a moment. / Casting off his faint, that virtuous hero Puṣkala, master of supreme missiles,
instantly cut to pieces with his arrows the skull-topped staff held in [Vīrabhadra's] hand. / When his skull-topped staff in his hand was broken, Vīrabhadra,
falling into supreme rage, smashed the chariot of the car-warrior. / Having smashed the hero's chariot and made him a foot-soldier,
he fought hand-to-hand combat with the high-souled Puṣkala. / Abandoning the chariot that had been crushed by him with great force,
the mighty Puṣkala struck Vīrabhadra with his fist. / Striking each other with fists, and likewise with thighs and knees,
eager to slay each other, desiring victory over one another, / in this manner four days passed, day and night, between the two lords.
Neither gave way, nor was the mighty [hero] conquered. / When the fifth day arrived, the mighty Vīrabhadra,
seizing the great hero Puṣkala, flew up into the sky. / There a duel took place between the two, confounding gods and demons,
a great fight with fists, kicks of the feet, arms, and claws. / Then, exceedingly enraged, Puṣkala seized Vīrabhadra
by the throat and slammed him onto the surface of the earth. / Pained by that blow, the mighty Vīrabhadra
seized Puṣkala by the foot and struck him, whirling him repeatedly; / having hurled Puṣkala against the earth, the exceedingly mighty one
swiftly severed his head, which had glowing earrings, with a trident. / Having slain Puṣkala, the mighty Vīrabhadra roared.
As that follower of Śarva roared, the formidable warriors were terrified; / a great lamentation arose when Puṣkala fell in battle.
All the people skilled in battle were terrified in the midst of the fight; / and they reported to Śatrughna that Puṣkala had fallen in the combat,
Slain indeed by Vīrabhadra, the attendant of Maheśvara. / Hearing then of the death of Puṣkala, the great hero
Fell into extreme sorrow on the battlefield, trembling greatly with grief. / And perceiving that Śatrughna was grieving, Rudra spoke these words
To the hero Śatrughna who was grieving in the encounter when Puṣkala was slain: / “O Śatrughna, do not grieve in battle, O you of exceedingly great strength!
For falling in the midst of battle is held to be a matter of renown for heroes. / Blessed is the hero named Puṣkala, who indeed for five days
Fought with Vīrabhadra, the maker of the great dissolution, / by whom in an instant Dakṣa, who had shown haughty disrespect, was slain,
And by whom in an instant the daityas, soldiers of Tripura, were slain. / Therefore fight, O king of kings, having cast away sorrow, O you of great strength!
Stand firmly today with effort, foremost of heroes, while I remain as your combatant!” / Casting aside sorrow, the heroic Śatrughna became enraged at Śaṅkara.
Taking up his readied bow, he covered Maheśvara with arrows. / Those arrows covered with wounds the body of the foremost of the gods,
Who had come to protect his devotee—which was a great wonder. / Those arrows and also the arrows of Śaṅkara, remaining in the sky,
Pervaded this whole universe, causing astonishment even to the sage. / Seeing the fighting power of the arrows of those two, everywhere they regarded it
As the dissolution that brings destruction to the world, stupefying everything. / Taking resort to aerial cars in the sky, those dwelling in their own realm,
Having come to watch, praised the two of them greatly: / “This one is the bringer of creation and dissolution to these three worlds,
And this other is the younger brother of the great king Rāmacandra. / What will come of this, or who will be victorious on the circle of the earth,
Or which hero will suffer defeat in the forefront of the battle?” / In this manner the combat between them went on for eleven days.
When the twelfth day arrived, the lord of men discharged a weapon / known as the Brahmā-weapon, filled with wrath, in order to slay Mahādeva.
Understanding that great weapon to have been discharged by his adversary Śatrughna, / he, even while smiling, swallowed that great Brahmaśiras discharged by him.
Having reached utter astonishment, thinking, “What is to be done after this?”— / while he was thus engaged in reflection, right into his heart
The crest-jewel of the gods of gods swiftly drove an arrow resembling fire. / By that arrow Śatrughna was rendered unconscious in the field of battle.
The entire army served by warriors became filled with cries of woe; / all the heroes were cast down upon the surface of the earth by Rudra’s attendants.
Proud of the strength of their own arms, Subāhu, Sumada, and the rest [were felled]. / Seeing Śatrughna fallen in a faint, tormented by the arrow,
And placing Puṣkala on a chariot to be guarded by attendants, / Hanūmān came to fight with Śiva, the cause of destruction,
Remembering Śrī Rāma, causing his own warriors to rejoice, O brāhmaṇa, / intensely angered and making his tail shake violently.

5.44.m: Śeṣa said: / Having approached Rudra in the forefront of the battlefield, / the heroic Hanumān spoke, desiring to slay the lord of the gods.
Hanūmān said: / “Since you act in opposition to dharma, O Rudra, / therefore I wish to punish you, who are intent on slaying the devotee of Rāma.
Formerly it was heard by me, O god, spoken in many ways by the sages, / that Rudra, the bearer of the Pināka, constantly remembers the feet of the lord of the Raghus.
All of that has become false, since you fight against Śatrughna. / My valiant Puṣkala has been slain, and Śatrughna too is rendered unconscious.
Therefore I shall strike you down today, who are intent upon the dissolution of the three worlds. / Stand firmly with effort, O Śarva, turned away from devotion to Rāma!”
Śeṣa said: / To the monkey who had spoken thus, Maheśvara said: / “Blessed are you, O best of heroes! You do not speak falsely.
Rāmacandra is my master, bowed to by gods and asuras. / Śatrughna, the slayer of enemy heroes, brought his horse;
I have come for the sake of his protection, overcome indeed by devotion to him. / Somehow or other this devotee is to be protected as one’s own self; such is the rule.
May the lord of the Raghus, having shown mercy, look upon me, who am shameless, / bearing a little anger on account of the great grief of his own devotee.”
Śeṣa said: / While the lord of Caṇḍī was speaking thus, Hanūmān, exceedingly enraged, / picked up a great boulder and struck his chariot.
Struck by the boulder, his chariot went to pieces, / along with the charioteer, the horses, the banner, and the flags.
All the deities standing in the sky praised the lord of monkeys: / “Blessed are you, O ruler of monkeys! A great deed has been done by you!”
Seeing Śrī Śiva deprived of his chariot, Nandī ran up to him / and said to Śrī Mahādeva, “Mount upon my back!”
And when the lord of beings was seated on the bull, Hanūmān, greatly enraged, / tore up a rock with speed and then struck him on the chest.
Then, being struck, the lord of beings took up a sharp trident, / blazing, three-pointed, equal in brilliance to flames of fire.
Seeing that great trident coming, blazing with light, / he seized it swiftly in his hand and instantly broke it into bits like sesame seeds.
When the trident was broken with speed in an instant by the king of monkeys, Śiva / took into his hand a spear entirely made of iron.
That spear discharged by Śiva struck the heart of that wise one, / and instantly the lord of monkeys became bewildered there.
And overcoming that pain in an instant, he seized a huge tree / and struck [him] on the chest adorned with great serpents.
Struck by that hero, the lords of serpents were overcome with terror; / leaving him, they fled here and there swiftly to Pātāla.
And Śiva, having seen that tree hurled upon his own chest, / became enraged and took a dread mace into his two hands:
“You are slain! Flee and run away from the battle, O lowest of monkeys! / Here in an instant I shall take your life with my mace!”
Seeing the club hurled by angry Śiva, / the monkey, remembering Hari, eluded it with great speed.
That mace made of great iron, discharged by Śiva, fell downward; / splitting the whole earth, it went to Rasātala.
Then Hanūmān, the servant of Rāma, exceedingly enraged, / took a mountain in his hand and struck [him] on the chest.
As long as the husband of Satī set his mind on splitting that mountain, / so long was he struck by the king of monkeys with a sāl tree having many branches.
As he prepared to split that as well, just so long was he struck by a boulder. / As Mṛḍa became intent on directing his mind to break those boulders,
Just so long did this one cause a rain of boulders, trees, and mountains; / and wrapping [him] with his tail, he struck the protector of beings.
With boulders, mountains, trees, and repeated lashings of his tail, / Nandī was filled with great terror, and the moon was shattered into pieces.
Maheśāna, prone to wrath, became exceedingly bewildered; / at every single moment, by blow after blow, he made him utterly distressed.
[Maheśāna] spoke to the lord of monkeys: “Blessed are you, follower of the lord of the Raghus! / A great deed was done by you today, by which I am well pleased.
Not by gift, nor by sacrifice, nor indeed by slight asceticism / am I easily reached, O one of great speed! Therefore, ask a boon of me.”
Śeṣa said: / Seeing him speaking thus, Hanūmān spoke to him, / smiling, with fearless speech, to the well-pleased Maheśāna.
Hanūmān said: / “By the grace of the lord of the Raghus, I have everything, O great lord! / Nevertheless, I ask a boon from you who are pleased in battle.
This Puṣkala of ours has fallen slain in battle, / and likewise Rāma's younger brother Śatrughna has swooned on the field.
And many other heroes have fallen, pierced with arrows; / some have swooned and fallen. Protect them together with your attendants,
so that great spirits, vetālas, and piśācas, / and likewise dogs, jackals, and others, do not carry them off or eat them.
Act so that there will be no mutilation of their bodies, / while I, having conquered Indra's host, carry off Mount Droṇa,
or, taking the medicinal herbs found there, restore the fallen warriors / and revive them all by my strength. Until then, protect them in every way.
Here I go to fetch Droṇa, that best of mountains, / upon which dwell the medicinal herbs that revive living beings.”
Having heard this speech, he replied to him, “So be it! / Go quickly to that mountain; I will protect your dead warriors.”
Having heard that word of the Lord, he went to Mount Droṇa; / crossing all the continents, he reached the Milk Ocean.
Now here the great Śiva, along with his own attendants, / was protecting that cremation ground with his own troops of great strength and prowess.
Hanūmān, having reached Droṇa, that great mountain named Droṇa, / placed it in his tail and swiftly set out toward the circle of battle.
When he strove to carry it off, O twice-born, that mountain trembled; / and seeing it trembling, the hosts of deities who guarded it
cried out, “Alas, alas!” and said, “What will happen to the mountain? / For who is this heroic one of great strength and prowess that is carrying it away?”
Having said so, all the gods gathered and saw the monkey; / shouting to him, “Release it!” they struck him with millions of weapons and missiles.
Seeing them all striking, Hanūmān was greatly enraged; / the hero struck them down in an instant, just as Śakra struck all the asuras.
Some there were struck by his foot, some crushed by his hand; / some were struck by his tail, and some were hit with a peak.
All met destruction, beaten down by the monkey in an instant; / some fell down upon the earth, bathed in blood.
Some, terrified through fear of the monkey, went to Śakra, the ruler of the gods, / scorched by wounds, their bodies injured by blood.
Seeing them agitated by fear and covered in blood, / the crestfallen Śakra, best of all the gods, addressed the gods:
“How are you terrified with fear? How are you bathed in blood? / By what Daitya or vile Rākṣasa were you struck down?
Tell me all that is true, so that, knowing it, I may go against him; / and having slain or bound your frantic slayer, I shall return.”
Having heard these words, the foremost of gods, in a plaintive voice, / addressed Indra, who is saluted by gods and asuras:
The gods said: / “Someone who has taken monkey form has come here—we do not know him; / he has undertaken to carry off Droṇa, having encircled that mountain with his tail.
Having made up his mind to go, all of us, closely united, / fought, fully equipped and showering all kinds of weapons and missiles.
All of us were completely defeated in battle by that powerful one; / many of the best of the gods fell there, slain, upon the earth.
We, however, survived by our many merits and have come here, / our limbs thoroughly drenched with blood, filled with the pain of our wounds.”
Having heard this speech of the gods, that Puraṃdara / commanded all the gods endowed with great strength:
“Go to the great Droṇa mountain to bind that monkey of great strength; / having bound him, bring that ruiner of the gods' battle!”
Commanded thus, they went indeed to Droṇa, the best of mountains, / where the strong hero Hanūmān, the best of monkeys, was staying.
Having gone, they all struck Hanūmān of great strength; / struck down by Hanūmān with fists and slaps of his hand,
they fell there in an instant, their bodies wounded with blood; / others, intent on flight, went to the lord of heaven.
Hearing that, Śakra was enraged; the best of the gods / ordered all the best immortals [against] the monkey lord, the great hero.
Commanded by him, they went to where the mighty monkey lord was; / seeing them all arrive, the best of monkeys said:
“Heroes, do not advance in battle against me who am your destroyer by force! / I will lead you now into the presence of the city of Saṃyaminī.”
Even though addressed thus, all of them, fully armed and endowed with mighty strength, / struck the monkey with numerous weapons and missiles discharged [at him].
some with spears and axes, some with swords and paṭṭiśas, / some with maces and javelins, turbid with anger.
Struck by the foremost immortals with diverse weapons, the mighty one / swiftly struck down all those best immortals with crags.
Some fled and, having gone near Śakra, reported [it]; / having heard that word spoken by them, the lord of the gods became afraid.
Going near Bṛhaspati, the superintendent of the gods, counselor to the heaven-dwellers, / he bowed to that excellent guru of the gods and asked:
Indra said: / “O master, who is that monkey who has come to carry off Droṇa, / by whom my heroic, weapon-bearing immortals have been slain?”
Śeṣa said: / Having heard that speech spoken [by him], the great Āṅgirasa / addressed the fear-agitated ruler of the gods, Turāṣāh.
Bṛhaspati said: / “He who killed Rāvaṇa in battle and consumed Kumbhakarṇa, / by whom all your enemies were slain—it is his servant indeed.
He by whom Laṅkā together with Mount Trikūṭa was burned with the fire of his tail, / and by whom Akṣa was killed—know him to be Hanūmān.
All have been struck down by him; he is striving for the sake of Droṇa. / The great king, best among the strong, is performing a horse sacrifice.
A great king devoted to Śiva, named Vīramaṇi, / seized his horse; there a battle bewildering to the gods took place.
Many heroes of Rāma were slain in the fight by Śiva; / in order to revive them, the very powerful one will certainly carry off Droṇa.
He, endowed with strength, cannot be conquered by you even in hundreds of years; / therefore propitiate the monkey, and give the medicine found there.”

5.45.m: Śeṣa said: / Hearing what the guru said, the independent ruler, enemy of Vṛṣaparvan, / knowing the son of the wind had come for the sake of Rāma's mission,
abandoned the fear that had arisen in his heart on account of the monkey; / his heart rejoiced exceedingly, and he spoke to Vācaspati:
Indra said: / “O lord of the gods, what should be done if this Droṇa is carried away? / How will the gods have their life again? Tell me that!”
Now propitiate the son of the wind properly, / so that Rāma will feel supreme pleasure and there will be happiness for the gods."
Hearing the words of the lord of the gods, Vācaspati then, / placing Śakra in front, surrounded by all the gods,
went there where the fearless monkey Hanumān was staying, / roaring violently after defeating all the gods who were sitting comfortably.
Having approached him, led by Bṛhaspati, / they indeed bowed and fell at the feet of the son of the wind.
And Bṛhaspati, the guru of the world, best of speakers, / urged by that lord of the gods, spoke to that hero:
"This act was done by the gods who did not know your valor. / You are the servant of Lord Rāma's feet, O high-minded one!
For what reason is this undertaking? Why have you come here? / We all, bowed low, shall carry out your bidding.
Cast off anger, show mercy, look upon the lord of the gods, / O son of the wind, who bear a form that brings terror to the Daityas!"
Śeṣa said: / Having heard the speech of the gods together with the words of their guru, / the greatly renowned one spoke thus to all the gods and their guru:
"In King Vīramaṇi's battle, numerous warriors were slain by Śarva; / to revive them, I shall carry away the Droṇa mountain.
Whoever, proud of their own prowess and strength, shall hinder me, / them I will send in a mere moment to Yama's abode.
Therefore, tell me of Droṇa or of that herb / with which I may revive the dead heroes on the battlefield."
Śeṣa said: / Having heard these words of the noble son of the wind, / they all bowed down and gave him the herb of revival.
Overjoyed, casting off fear, the gods, dwellers of heaven, / went their way with the lord of the gods in front, filled with happiness.
Hanumān, taking that herb, came to the battle, / praised by all the hosts of gods who were eager for the great deed.

Seeing that Hanumān had arrived, even all the enemies, / praising him, 'Well done! Well done!', considered the monkey wonderful.

The monkey, having arrived, full of great joy, / [saw] before him the warrior Puṣkala, who had met his death.
guarded by Śiva in the terrible circle [of battle], / went near him, his mind set on Lord Rāma.
And summoning the minister Sumati, who was esteemed by the great, / he said: "Today I shall revive all the heroes dead in battle."
Having spoken thus, placing that herb on Puṣkala's broad chest / and joining the head with the torso, he uttered auspicious words:
"If in mind, speech, and deed I know Rāghava as my master, / then by this herb let him quickly live!"
Just as he was speaking these words, Puṣkala arose; / on the battlefield, the crest-jewel among heroes bit his teeth in wrath.
"Where has that Vīrabhadra gone, after making me faint on the battlefield? / Instantly I shall strike him down! Where is my excellent bow?"
As he was speaking thus, the lord of monkeys said to that hero: / "Blessed are you, hero, that you speak thus again on the battlefield!"
You were slain by Vīrabhadra, and by the grace of the lord of the Raghus / you are revived. Come, let us go to Śatrughna who has fainted."
Having said this, he went there to the forefront of the great battle; / there Śatrughna lay gasping, afflicted by Śiva's arrows.
Going there near to that high-minded Śatrughna, / placing the herb on his chest as his breath was returning,
Hanumān said to him: "Live, O best of Śatrughnas! / Why have you fainted in battle, O you of great strength and valor?
If I have diligently observed celibacy from my birth onwards, / then let the heroic Śatrughna revive this instant!"
As soon as this was spoken by him, he was revived in a mere moment: / "Where is Śiva? Where has Śiva gone, abandoning the battlefield?"
The many heroes who were slain in battle by the revered Rudra, wielder of the Pināka, / were all revived by the high-minded lord of monkeys.
Then, all well-equipped, their minds filled with wrath, / mounted on their respective chariots, their wounds healed, they advanced against the enemies.
Puṣkala [fought] against Vīrabhadra, and Kuśadhvaja against Caṇḍa, / the heroic Hanumān against Nandin, and Śatrughna against Śiva in battle.
The king advanced toward that Śatrughna, the best of the strong, / who was twanging his bow and standing challenging Śiva to battle.
King Vīramaṇi the hero and Śatrughna the mighty / fought a duel in battle that caused astonishment to the sages.
And by King Vīramaṇi, more than a hundred chariots / of the lord of men Śatrughna were shattered to pieces in an instant, O twice-born.
Then Śatrughna became exceedingly enraged on the battlefield; / he released the weapon of fire to burn him along with his army.
Seeing that great flaming missile released by the enemy, / the king, exceedingly enraged, seized the weapon of Varuṇa.
Seeing [his army] afflicted by cold due to the weapon of Varuṇa, Rāma's mighty younger brother / released the weapon of Vāyu; by it a great wind arose.
Dispersed by the wind, the clouds drifted in every direction; / they all scattered here and there, and that army appeared relieved.
When his army was troubled by the wind, the great King Vīramati / took up on his bow the mountain-weapon that repels foes.
The wind was checked by the mountains and did not move forward in battle; / seeing that, Rāma's younger brother took up the thunderbolt-weapon.
All those mountains were struck by the thunderbolt-weapon and cut into pieces like sesame seeds; / they were pulverized in that battle honored by excellent heroes.
With their bodies torn open by the thunderbolt-missile, heroes adorned with blood / lay at the edge of the battlefield; the combat became wondrous.
Then, exceedingly enraged, the great King Vīramaṇi / fitted to his bow the Brahmā-weapon, wonderful, burning the enemy.
Śatrughna took an arrow and remembered the very captivating / weapon given by the Yoginī, which confounds all enemies.
As that Brahmā-weapon, released from the hand, approached toward the enemy, / just then the weapon of stupefaction was released by the one named Śatrughna.
By the weapon of stupefaction, that Brahmā-weapon was cut in two in an instant here; / it quickly struck the king's chest, causing the king to swoon.
Hundreds of arrows were released by King Śatrughna; / all the heroes, the attendants of Rudra, fainted again.
Stupefied, they fell to the earth at Śiva's feet; / then Śiva, greatly enraged, standing in his chariot, approached the king.
Śatrughna, who had come to the battlefield to fight swiftly with Śiva, / made ready his bow with its string drawn, and fought.
Between the two occurred a dreadful battle, tearing apart enemies, / illuminating the quarters of the sky with weapons and missiles loosed in abundance.
With clashes of missile against missile, with blows and counter-blows, / not even among the gods and Daityas had there been such a battlefield.
Then Śatrughna, exceedingly distressed in combat with Śiva, / remembered his Lord there, following the counsel of the son of Pavana:
"Alas, Lord! O brother! Extremely fierce Śiva, raising his bow, / is taking away my life; protect me on the battlefield!
Many have crossed the ocean of sorrow through your name, O Rāma; / deliver me too who am plunged in sorrow, O Rāma, O Rāma, ocean of compassion!"
Just as he was speaking thus, Rāma was seen on the battlefield, / dark as a blue lotus petal, lotus-eyed,
holding an antelope horn at his waist, bearing the consecrated body [of a sacrificer]. / Seeing him, Śatrughna was filled with wonder on the battlefield.

5.46.m: Śeṣa said: / Seeing glorious Rāma arrive, who removes the distress of the bowed, / Śatrughna, [seeing] his brother, was freed from all sorrow, O best of the twice-born.
Seeing him, Hanūmān, deeply moved, gladly bowed to Rāma's feet, / who had come to protect his devotee, and said:
"O Lord, it is indeed fitting for you to protect your devotee, / since you have freed everyone conquered in battle and bound in nooses.
We are indeed blessed now, for we shall behold your feet; / we shall conquer our enemies in an instant by your grace, O descendant of Raghu."
Śeṣa said: / Sthāṇu [Śiva] then fell at the feet of Rāma who had come, who is accessible to the meditation of yogins, / and said [to him] who grants fearlessness to those who bow:
"You alone are proclaimed the manifest Puruṣa, beyond material nature, / who create, protect, and destroy the universe by a portion of your own fraction.
Formless yourself, you are the supreme cause of the entire universe; / though one alone, you assume a threefold form through your illusory power.
In creation [you appear] in the form of the creator [Brahmā], in preservation you yourself remain [as Viṣṇu], / and in the destruction of the universe, I directly have assumed the name Śarva.
That you, the Supreme Lord, perform the rite of the horse sacrifice / to dispel the murder of a brahmin—that is a wondrous mimicry.
The pure washing of your feet named Gaṅgā, I bear upon my head / to quell sin—how could there be sin in you?
Clearly, an action has been done by me to cause you much offense; / let that be forgiven, O compassionate one, for it stood in your way.
What could I do? This was done by me to protect my truth. / Knowing your majesty, I came to protect my devotee.
Formerly, in Ujjayinī, at the abode of Mahākāla, / this man bathed in the river named Śiprā and performed most wondrous asceticism.
Then, being pleased, I spoke to the king: / 'Choose [a boon], O great king.' And he chose an astonishing kingdom.
I said: 'Your kingdom will be in Devapura / until Rāma's sacrificial horse arrives in the city.
From then on, I shall remain ready to protect you.' / Having granted this boon, O Rāma, what could I do on account of my truth?
Now I am held in regard by the king along with his sons, animals, and kinsmen; / handing over the horse, the king will render service to your feet."
Śeṣa said: / Hearing this speech of Maheśa, the best of the Raghus / spoke in a steady voice, his eyes full of compassion.
Rāma said: / "This alone is the duty of the gods: the protection of a devotee. / You have performed an excellent deed, since your devotee has now been protected.
You are in my heart, O Śarva, and I am in your heart. / There is no difference between us; fools of wicked intellect perceive [a distinction].
Those men who truly make a distinction between us who are of one form / are cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hells for a thousand kalpas.
Those who are your devotees are indeed my devotees, endowed with dharma; / my devotees also offer bows to you with immense devotion."
Śeṣa said: / Hearing what was spoken thus, the lord Śarva brought King Vīramaṇi, / who was unconscious, back to life by the touch of his hand and other means.
His other sons too, unconscious and tormented by arrows, / the gracious, capable, and sovereign lord brought back to life.
Having restored the king, the lord of beings made him bow / at glorious Rāma's feet, surrounded by his sons and grandsons.
Blessed was King Vīramaṇi who beheld the best of the Raghus, / difficult to attain even by countless tens of thousands of yogins steadfast in yoga.
Because of that [sight of] the lord of the Raghus, their bodies attained fulfillment / and they became most worthy of worship by Brahmā and the others, O best of the twice-born.
To Rāma, praised by Śatrughna and Hanumān / and by fierce [warriors] headed by Puṣkala, the king gave the best of horses.
King Vīramaṇi then surrendered everything along with his kingdom, / including sons, cattle, and kinsmen, urged by Śarva.
Then Rāma, praised by all, by former enemies and his own servants, / and especially by Śatrughna and the others who were intensely eager,
disappeared while standing in his chariot made of jewels. / When auspicious Rāma disappeared, everyone was filled with great astonishment.
Do not consider him a mere human, that Rāma who is worshipped by all the worlds; / in water, on land, everywhere, he resides always established.
Then the warriors, exceedingly delighted, embraced one another; / with auspicious musical instruments and trumpets, a great festival took place.
Then the horse was released by all the heroes skilled in weapons and missiles, / followed by all, who were joyful and filled with wonder.
Śarva, true to his vow, took leave of his servant, / saying: 'Go to glorious Rāma, difficult to attain in all the worlds, as your refuge.'
The cause of universal dissolution and origination himself disappeared there; / Śarva went to Kailāsa, resplendent with his attendants.
King Vīramaṇi, meditating on the lotus feet of glorious Rāma, / went together with powerful Śatrughna, accompanied by his army.
Those best of men who hear this deed of Rāma / will never suffer sorrow born of worldly existence.

5.47.m: Śeṣa said: / Then, O twice-born, the horse went to Hemakūṭa at the border of Bhārata, / protected by many thousands of soldiers, adorned with tied chowries,
which was ten thousand yojanas in width and length all around, / with beautiful peaks of silver, gold, and other [metals].
There was a great, excellent park, resplendent with trees: / with śāla, tāla, tamāla, and karṇikāra trees all around,
with hintāla, nāga, punnāga, kovidāra along with bilva, / campaka, bakula, megha, madana, kuṭaja, and others,
adorned with jāti, yūthikā, and navamālikā jasmines, / mangoes, mādhavī creepers, vines of grapes, and pomegranates—a magnificent forest,
resounding with numerous birds, filled with the buzzing of bees, / echoing with the calls of peacocks, granting delight in all seasons. The horse
entered it, possessing the speed of the mind, / bearing an enchanting gold plaque on his broad forehead, followed by Śatrughna.
As that mount of the horse sacrifice was going along, / suddenly an extraordinary thing occurred; listen to that, O best of the twice-born.
A paralysis of the limbs came upon him; standing on the path, he did not move; / like Hemakūṭa itself, the excellent horse became immovable.
Then all his guardians struck him with whips; / yet even when struck, the best of horses did not move, his limbs stiffened.
Going near to Śatrughna, the guardians of the horse cried out: / "O lord, we do not know what has happened to the excellent horse.
As the best of horses was proceeding with the speed of thought, O king, / a sudden paralysis of his limbs occurred, O wise one!"
Struck by us with whips, yet he did not move an inch from there. / Considering this, do whatever action is fit, O best of kings."
Then, seized with astonishment, the king, together with all his soldiers, / went to the vicinity of the great horse.
Puṣkala, seizing the horse's two feet from the ground with his arms, / tried to lift them up, but they did not move from there.
Overcome by force by the mighty warrior, the horse still did not tremble then. / The high-minded Hanūmat made up his mind to pull him up.
Enfolding [him] with his tail, the best among the strong / dragged the steed forcefully by his strength; yet he did not stir.
Then Hanūmat, the best of monkeys, filled with amazement, / spoke to Śatrughna, the foremost of the strong, as the heroes listened:
"Just recently, Mount Droṇa was uprooted by me with my tail in sport, / yet a great wonder is here: this small horse does not even tremble!
Indeed, a root cause is seen here; pulled though he is by mighty and furious warriors, / he has not moved even a sesame seed's breadth from his spot."
Hearing the speech of the monkey, Śatrughna, filled with wonder, / the best among speakers, addressed Sumati, the foremost of ministers:
Śatrughna said: / "O minister, why has this paralysis of the body occurred to the steed, O sinless one? / What means should be adopted here by which movement may come to the steed?"
Sumati said: / "O lord, some sage skilled in all knowledge must be sought out. / I know what arises from this land, perceptible to the senses, not what is beyond perception."
Śeṣa said: / Hearing this speech of Sumati, [the king], knowing what is right, / searched for a virtuous sage along with his servants.
Going everywhere, all those warriors looking everywhere / for a sage who knows dharma did not see any lord of sages.
One attendant, however, O brāhmaṇa, having gone just a yojana / in the eastern direction, looking eagerly, beheld a great hermitage,
where all the beasts and people were free from enmity, / charming, with all their sins destroyed by bathing in the Gaṅgā;
where some were performing excellent austerities with fires, / hanging head-down in smoke, filling their bellies with leaves and air;
where smoke born of the fire sacrifice constantly purifies, / delighting many sages, and excellent vines drop leaves [at their feet].
Knowing that charming hermitage to belong to the sage Śaunaka, / he reported it to the king whose mind was filled with wonder.
Hearing that, exceedingly pleased, Śatrughna with his servants / and accompanied by Hanūmat, Puṣkala, and the rest, went to that hermitage.
Seeing the foremost sage there, who had duly offered oblations into the sacrificial fire, / and having bowed down like a staff to his sin-destroying feet,
knowing the king to have arrived, Śatrughna the foremost of the strong, / [the sage] offered water for hospitality and feet; he was pleased by the sight of him.
To the king comfortably seated and rested, the lord of sages said: / "For what purpose is this wandering, your great journeying, O lord?
If kings like you, O son of Vena, do not wander the entire earth, / then wicked people afflict the righteous who are free from fever.
Speak, O protector of the earth, Śatrughna, foremost among the strong! / May your wandering and all else turn out for the good of us all."
Śeṣa said: / To the brāhmaṇa who spoke thus, the lord of the earth replied, / his body thrilled with joy, with a voice choked with emotion:
Śatrughna said: / "A sudden wonder has occurred to Rāma's captivating horse / not far from your dwelling; hear of it, O foremost of the wise!
By chance, the horse went into your lovely garden; / at its edge, a bodily paralysis overtook that steed in an instant.
Then my mighty warriors, Puṣkala and the rest, fierce with pride, / pulled the steed by force, yet he did not move.
You are considered a boat to us who are sunk in a boundless ocean of sorrow; / you have been seen by providence through good fortune; tell us the cause!"
Śeṣa said: / Asked thus, the excellent sage of great intellect meditated for a moment; / then, holding the horse in his mind, he investigated the cause.
In a moment, attaining knowledge of that, his eyes wide with wonder, / he spoke to the earth-protector who was sorrowful and filled with doubt:
Śaunaka said: / "Listen, O king, I shall declare the cause of the horse's paralysis, / hearing which very wonderful tale one is freed from sorrow.
In the Gauḍa country, in a great forest adorned by the banks of the Kāverī, / a brāhmaṇa named Sātvaka practiced supreme asceticism.
For one day he drank milk; for one day he ate air; / and for one day he remained without food: thus he passed three days at a time.
While he was engaged in such a vow, Time, which causes the destruction of all things, / seized him in its fangs; the keeper of great vows met his death.
On an aerial chariot endowed with all beauty and adorned with all jewels, / sporting with apsarases, he went to dwell on the peak of Meru.
There was a great jambu tree there whose juice was delicious to drink; / and a river named Jāmbavatī, filled with molten gold,
in which sages sported at will, filled with curiosity, / holy through much asceticism, endowed with all happiness.
Sporting there at his pleasure with apsarases, filled with delight, / haughty with the intoxication of his own pride, he acted against them.
Then he was cursed by the sages: 'Become a rākṣasa, Durmukha!' / Then, exceedingly sorrowful, he spoke to the sages whose wealth was knowledge and asceticism:
'May you all, compassionate brāhmaṇas, show grace to me!' / Then he was granted a favor by them: 'When you
shall paralyze Rāma's horse by force, then the hearing of the story of Rāma, / and afterward liberation from this dreadful curse, will come to you.'
Having attained rakṣasa-hood, spoken of by the sages, that god-like one, O lord, / paralyzed Rāma's horse; liberate him, O sinless one, through recitations!"

5.48.m: Śeṣa said: / Having fully heard what was spoken by the sage, the slayer of enemy heroes / felt wonder in his heart and spoke to Śaunaka:
Śatrughna said: / "Unfathomable is the working of action, by which he who bore the name Sātvaka, / though having attained heaven, was turned into a rākṣasa by a mighty deed!
O lord, speak, O great ṛṣi, how actions reach their course, / [and] through the fruition of what action what kind of hell arises."
Śaunaka said: / "You are blessed, O best of the Raghus, in that you have this noble intention; / though knowing it, you ask for the benefit of the worlds, O sir!
I shall declare the diverse courses of manifold deeds; / listen to them, O great king, hearing which one attains liberation.
That evil-minded man who, with a desire for enjoyment, takes by force / another's wealth, another's child, and another's wife,
bound by the snare of Time by the mighty messengers of Yama, / is cast into the Tāmisra hell for as long as a thousand years.
