There the servants of Yama, raising [their weapons], beat him; / tormented by the experience of evil deeds, he then [enters] the womb of a sow.
Having suffered great agony there, he will attain human birth, / marked there by diseases and the like, which indicate his ill-fame."
He who solely supports his own family by doing injury to living beings, / devoted to sin, falls into Andhatāmisra.
Those men who indeed falsely slaughter living creatures in this world / are cast down into Raurava and torn to pieces in fury by rurus.
He who openly slaughters living beings for the sake of his own belly, / however, is cast by the command of Yama into the hell named Mahāraurava.
The evildoer who hates a brāhmaṇa, the progenitor of living beings, / [falls] into Kālasūtra, extremely dreadful, extending for ten thousand yojanas.
He who harbors hatred against cattle is cooked by Yama's servants / for as many thousands of years as there are hairs on the beast.
A king on earth who punishes one who does not deserve punishment, / and who, out of greed, also inflicts bodily punishment on a brāhmaṇa,
is tormented by the cruel servants of Yama possessing boar faces; / afterwards, he is born into wicked wombs for liberation from his sin.
Those men who out of delusion seize the wealth, conduct, or slight livelihood / or subsistence of brāhmaṇas and cows, and tear it away by their own power,
are cast into Andhakūpa in the other world and severely afflicted. / One who procures sweet food for himself and greedily eats it,
giving none to the gods nor to a friend, intent on the pleasures of the tongue, / falls indeed into the hell named Kṛmibhojana.
The man who, outside of an emergency, steals gold and the like, / or the property of a brāhmaṇa, falls into the very wicked Saṃdaṃśa hell.
The dull-witted one who nourishes his own body and cares for no other / is cast into the exceedingly terrible Kumbhīpāka, boiling with oil.
The man who, out of delusion and longing for female form, desires a woman who should not be approached— / him Yama's servants force to embrace a red-hot iron image of her.
Those who violently break the bounds of the Veda, puffed up by their own strength, / fallen into the Vaitaraṇī river, are eaters of flesh and blood.
He who takes a Śūdra woman as his first wife and practices householdership with her / falls into Pūyoda, filled with intense suffering.
The rogues who resort to hypocrisy to deceive the world, / those fools fall into the Vaiśasa hell, beaten by Yama.
Those fools who make a woman of equal class drink their own semen, / those sinners, intent on drinking semen, [fall] into rivers of semen.
Those wicked thieves, arsonists, poisoners, and plunderers of villages, / laden with sins, are cast down into Sārameyādana.
A man filled with sin who gives false testimony, / or who, being powerful, forcibly steals the property of another,
that sinner falls headlong downward into the Avīci hell; / having experienced great suffering there, he enters a most sinful womb.
The dull-witted man who drinks liquor for the pleasure of the tongue, / him the servants of Dharmarāja force to drink molten iron.
The man who disdains his gurus, arrogant on account of his learning and conduct, / when dead, is cast head downward into the Kṣāra hell.
Those men who commit a breach of trust, devoid of dharma, / are cast into the Śūlaprota hell with much torture.
The slanderous man who agitates all people with his words, / having fallen into Dandaśūka, is bitten constantly by biting serpents.
Thus, O King, there are indeed many hells for evildoers; / having committed sin, they go there and undergo exceedingly dreadful torment.
For those by whom the story of Rāma was not heard and by whom no benefit was rendered to others, / all kinds of suffering occur within the hells.
Now it will be spoken how there may be happiness in heaven for someone, / and also [concerning] those who, full of suffering and disease, have returned from hell.
Śeṣa said: / Having heard this, the king, trembling at every moment, / asked the brāhmaṇa once again in order to dispel all doubt:
Tell, O great sage, the signs of those various sins: / by which sin what sign arises in the world of mortals?
Having heard those words, the sage said to the king: / "Listen, O king, I will proclaim the signs of evildoers."
Śaunaka said: / “A drinker of liquor is born with black teeth after hell; / and one who eats inedible things is born with an abdominal tumor.
Having eaten food seen by a menstruating woman, one is born with worms in the belly; / having eaten food touched by dogs, cats, and the like, one becomes foul-smelling.
A man eating without offering to the gods and others is born / diseased in the stomach, miserable, afflicted by severe illness.
Indigestion arises from obstructing another's food; / one who gives bad food when wealth is available gets sluggish digestive fire.
A poisoner becomes one who suffers from vomiting; an obstructor of paths gets foot disease; / a slanderer, at the end of hell, is born with asthma and cough.
A rogue becomes epileptic; one who torments others suffers from colic; / and an incendiary of forest fires becomes afflicted with bloody diarrhea.
He who casts feces into a temple or into water / gets an extremely dreadful rectal disease, the very embodiment of his sin.
Diseases born from causing abortion are consumption, urinary disorders, and dropsy; / and a breaker of sacred images is born without standing.
A malicious speaker becomes mutilated; a slanderer of others becomes bald; / and one who shows partiality in an assembly is born with paralysis.
One who mocks another's speech is one-eyed; a stealer of a brāhmaṇa's gold has deformed nails; / a thief of copper becomes pot-bellied; a stealer of bronze gets white leprosy.
A man who steals tin is born with reddish-brown hair; / a man who steals lead is born with diseases of the head.
A man who is a thief of ghee is born with eye disease; / and a man who steals iron is born with deformed limbs.
A man who steals leather is born covered in excessive fat; / a man who is a thief of honey is born with a smell like a goat.
By the theft of oil a man becomes severely afflicted with scabies; / and from taking raw grain he is born toothless.
From taking cooked food he becomes afflicted with diseases of the tongue; / and a man who sleeps with his mother is born without a penis.
From approaching the wife of a guru, painful urination arises; / and when going to a sister, yellow leprosy is born.
Upon approaching one's own daughter, red leprosy arises; / upon approaching a brother's wife, nodular leprosy arises.
Upon having intercourse with one belonging to one's master, ringworm arises; / upon approaching the wife of a trusting friend, elephantiasis arises.
Upon approaching a father's sister, one becomes afflicted with sores on the right side of the body; / but upon approaching a maternal uncle's wife, one has sores on the left side of the body.
Upon approaching a paternal uncle's wife, leprosy arises on the hips; / upon approaching a friend's wife, one is born whose wife dies.
By intercourse with a woman of one's own clan, fistula in ano arises; / by intercourse with a female ascetic, urinary disease arises in a man.
By intercourse with the wife of a learned Vedic brāhmaṇa, one is born with a sore on the nose; / by intercourse with the wife of an initiated person, one discharges corrupt blood.
Upon having intercourse with a woman of one's own caste, one is born with an ulcer in the heart; / upon intercourse with a woman of a higher caste, one is born with an ulcer on the head.
From having intercourse with an animal womb, retention of urine arises; / these defects belong to men at the conclusion of hell, there is no doubt.
These also occur in women from association with those respective men. / In this way, O King, the signs of extreme sinners have been related.
Through association with charitable giving and merit, and likewise by actions such as [visiting] sacred places, / having heard the life of Rāma, or through austerity, [sin] goes to destruction.
The river of the fame of Hari washes away the mire of all sins / of evil-doing men; no hesitation should be made in this regard.”

If someone scorns Hari, even his sacrifices enjoined by the scriptures
and the most holy tirthas are not able to purify him.

Whoever, feeble in wisdom, derides [his] deeds being proclaimed,
he will have no release from hell even at the end of a kalpa.

Go, O king, for the sake of the horse's liberation, along with your attendants;
make [him] hear the deeds of the Lord of Śrī, whereby the steed may attain [free] motion."

Going there, beside the best of horses,
he recited the deeds of Rāma, which destroy great misfortune:

"Go to your own divine aerial vehicle by the merit of praising Rāma;
wander freely in your own realm, and be released from your base rebirth!"
Having heard these words, as Śatrughna was seated, / he saw a pure, excellent god in a celestial chariot.

He said: "I am liberated through hearing the recitation of Rāma's praises;
I go to my own abode, O noble-minded king! Give me leave."
Having said this, the god departed, seated in his celestial chariot; / then Śatrughna along with his followers was filled with wonder.

Then the steed, freed from the paralysis of its limbs and from the ground,
went through that whole forest, wandering among crowded birds.

5.49.m:
Śeṣa said:
Seven months passed as that best of horses, in sport,
wandered across the continent of Bhārata, filled with many kings.

Honored by the best of kings, traversing the noble Bhārata,
surrounded by the best of heroes, the mighty Śatrughna and others,

it wandered through many lands near the Himālayas;
remembering the might of Rāma, no one captured the horse.

Praised by the kings of the Aṅgas, Vaṅgas, and Kaliṅgas, the horse
arrived at the delightful city of King Suratha,

a city named Kuṇḍala, where the earring of Aditi,
shaking with great joy and fear, had fallen from her ears onto the earth.

There no man ever transgresses dharma;
with love the people remember Śrī Rāma every day.

There worship of the holy fig trees and of the tulasī is performed daily
by men, sinless servants of Raghunātha.

There lovely temples containing images of Rāghava
are daily worshipped by people of pure heart, free from deceit.

There Hari's name is on the tongue, not talk of strife;
meditation upon him alone is in the heart, and not thought of selfish fruits.

There the play of those whose bodies are purified by tales of Rāma
is never that of men who pride themselves on the vice of false speech.

In that place dwelt the righteous Suratha, truthful and strong,
his heart gladdened by remembering the feet of Raghunātha, supremely ecstatic.

How can I describe that excellent Suratha, servant of Rāma,
whose boundless virtues, renowned throughout the earth, purify sin?

Once the servants of that king, while roaming about,
saw the horse of the horse sacrifice smeared with sandalwood paste.

Filled with wonder at seeing it, they read the horse's inscribed plate,
inscribed with clear letters and anointed with sandalwood and the like.

Knowing the horse, delight of the eyes, to have been set loose by Rāma,
they were rejoiced and eagerly reported to the king sitting in his assembly:

"O master, the lord of the city of Ayodhyā is Rāghava;
the wandering horse fit for his horse sacrifice has been released.

Accompanied by attendants, it has arrived near your city;
O great king, seize that most delightful horse!"

Śeṣa said:
Hearing these words spoken by his own people, overflowing with joy,
he spoke to the mighty warriors with a voice deep as thunder:

Suratha said:
"Blessed are we; together with our servants we shall see Rāma's face!
I shall capture his horse, though it is surrounded by ten million soldiers.

Then, only when Rāma comes here, will I release the steed,
so that I, his devotee, long engrossed in meditating on him, may be fulfilled."

Śeṣa said:
Having spoken thus, the ruler of the earth instructed his servants himself:
"Seize the steed by force; once in sight, the horse must not be released!

From this, in my view, there will be a very great gain:
that I may behold Rāma's feet, difficult to attain even for Brahmā, Indra, and the rest.

Blessed indeed is that kinsman, son, or relative,
or animal, or mount, by which the attainment of Rāma may occur.

Therefore, seize the sacrificial horse adorned with the gold plate,
swift as desire and pleasing to the mind, and bind it in the stable!"
Having been spoken to thus, they went from there, seized Rāma's splendid horse / with haste, and brought it, endowed with every auspicious mark, to the king.

The king, destroyer of demons, having gladly received Rāma's horse,
spoke to his mighty servants, skilled in works of righteousness:

"O Vātsyāyana of great intellect, listen with an attentive mind!
In his realm no man was devoted to another's wife,

nor intent on another's property, nor dissolute in lusts,
nor devoted on their tongues to improper ways, [all] because of singing Rāma's praises.

The king said to the servants: "You have come for service;
speak of your conduct, O men skilled in duties of righteousness!

Do the soldiers observe the vow of devotion to a single wife, not coveting others' wealth,
not intent on slandering others, and not following paths contrary to the Veda?

Do they daily practice remembering Śrī Rāma and the like?
For the sake of serving Rāma, I, fierce as Yama, protect them.

Those men of contrary conduct who are attached to sin,
such evil-minded people I do not allow to dwell in my realm."

In his country, even the most sinful did not commit sin in thought,
all their sins destroyed by meditation on Hari, filled with joy.

When the land was like this, and the king was united with righteousness,
then all men dwelling there, upon dying, attained supreme bliss.

There was no entrance for the messengers of Yama into the city of Suratha;
then Yama, assuming the form of an ascetic, approached the lord of the earth.

Wearing bark garments, his head adorned with matted hair,
he saw Suratha, the servant of Hari, in the midst of the assembly,

with tulasī upon his head, the supreme name of Hari on his tongue,
and expounding to his own people discourse devoted to acts of righteousness.

Then, seeing the sage standing like asceticism incarnate,
the king bowed at his feet and offered water for washing his feet and the rest.

To the sage comfortably seated and rested, the foremost of kings said:
"Blessed is my birth today, blessed is my house today!

Tell me the various excellent stories of Rāma,
by hearing which, destruction of sins will occur at every step."

Hearing this spoken, that sage laughed loudly,
showing all his teeth and clapping his hands.

To that laughing sage he said: "What is the reason for your laughter?
Tell me by your favor, so that my mind may find joy."

Then the sage said to the king: "Listen with understanding, O king,
as I tell you the excellent reason for my smile.

You said, 'Speak of Hari's glory before me';
who is Hari, or whose is glory? All men are subject to karma."
"By action heaven is obtained, by action one goes to hell. / By action alone everything comes about: many sons, grandsons, and the rest.
Śakra, having performed a hundred sacrifices, went to the highest place; / and Brahmā too, by action, obtained the wondrous world called Satya.
Many lords, such as the Maruts, perfected by action, / enjoy pleasures and happiness, served by hosts of Apsarases.
Therefore perform sacrifices and the like; worship the gods! / So that your stainless renown will spread across the earth."
Having heard those words, his mind agitated by anger, / he, whose mind was solely devoted to Rāma, spoke to the brāhmaṇa skilled in rituals:
"Do not speak talk of action, which gives perishable fruits! / Go outside my city's outskirts, reviled by the world!
Indra will soon fall, and the lotus-born [Brahmā] too will fall; / but men eager to worship Rāma will never fall.
"Look at Dhruva, and Prahlāda, and the wondrous Vibhīṣaṇa, / and whichever others are devoted to Rāma—they never fall."
Those wicked ones who revile Rāma—the servants of Yama / will beat them with iron clubs and bind them in nooses.
Because of your brāhmaṇahood, I will not inflict corporal punishment on you, lowest of the twice-born! / Go, go from my sight, or else I will strike [you]!"
When the noble king named Suratha had spoken thus, / his servants took [the brāhmaṇa] by the arm, prepared to throw him out.
Then Yama assumed his own form, praised by the entire world, / and said to the king: "I am pleased! Ask a boon, servant of Hari!
Though tempted by me with many words, O man of good vows, / you were not moved from the service of Rāma, which is practiced by the virtuous."
Then the lord of the earth, seeing Yama well pleased, / spoke and said: "If you are pleased, grant me an excellent boon:
May I have no death until my meeting with Rāma; / and let there never be fear for me from you, O Dharmarāja!"
Then Yama said to the king: "This will be yours! / The lord of Raghu's line will fulfill all your desires as true."
Having spoken thus, Dharma vanished and went to his own city, / praising the conduct of that supreme soul devoted to Hari.
That righteous king, servant of Rāma, with supreme joy, / having seized the horse, said to his servants, servants of Hari:
"I have seized this steed of King Rāghava! / Everywhere be prepared, all of you skilled in battle!"
Addressed in this manner, all those mighty warriors of the king / were ready in an instant and went eagerly into the assembly.
The king's ten heroic sons—Campaka, and Mohaka, / Ripuñjaya, the irresistible, the majestic Balamodaka,
Haryakṣa, Sahadeva, Bhūrideva, and Sutāpana— / thus the king's ten sons made ready on the battleground.
Endowed with great vigor, they formed the desire to march forth. / The king too summoned his wondrous chariot, fashioned with the splendor of gold,
adorned with swift horses. / Filled with enthusiasm for battle, surrounded by all his army,
the king sat in the assembly giving commands to all his servants.

5.50.m: Śeṣa said: / Then the younger brother of Rāma [Śatrughna], having arrived in haste, / asked his servants: "Where is that very charming sacrificial horse?"
Then those very mighty warriors spoke these words to Śatrughna: / "We do not know; some soldiers took the horse and went into the city.
And we were all humiliated by the king's strong servants. / In this matter, your lordship is the authority on what must be done."
Hearing their words, Śatrughna became exceedingly enraged; / biting his teeth in anger, repeatedly licking his lips with his tongue,
the hero said: "Having stolen my steed, where will you go? / Now I shall bring down the city along with its people with my arrows!"
Having said this, he spoke to Sumati: "Whose city is this? / Who is its ruler that took away my horse?"
Śeṣa said: / Hearing this speech of the king filled with wrath, / the minister spoke in an eloquent voice, with clear syllables:
"Know that this very charming city is named Kuṇḍala. / In it dwells the righteous and powerful kṣatriya Suratha,
"Always intent on righteousness, a servant of both of Rāma's feet / in mind, deed, and speech, a servant like Hanūmān."
There are hundreds of righteous deeds done by him; / Suratha is fully magnificent, with a very strong retinue.
A great battle will take place here if the excellent horse has been taken; / many heroes skilled in battle will fall."
Hearing what was said thus to the minister, / Śatrughna, the best of speakers, again spoke these words:
Śatrughna said: / "What should be done here if Rāma's horse has been taken by him? / He does not come to fight against a powerful army attended by heroes."
Sumati said: / "O great king, an eloquent envoy should be sent to the king, / by whose word the best of the strong will come with his force.
Otherwise, if the horse was seized out of ignorance by someone proud, / he will duly restore the auspicious, excellent sacrificial horse to us."
Having heard those words, the wise and mighty Śatrughna / spoke these words, filled with courtesy, to Aṅgada:
Śatrughna said: / "Go to the great city of Suratha situated near here; / having gone there as an envoy, speak to the king:
'Whether Rāma's horse was seized by you knowingly or unknowingly, / let him return it, or let him come to the battle accompanied by his warriors!'
Act just as you did as Rāma's envoy to Rāvaṇa in Laṅkā, / O intelligent one endowed with abundant strength!"
Śeṣa said: / Hearing this, the heroic Aṅgada said 'So be it' to the king, / and went into the midst of the assembly filled with ranks of warriors.
He saw King Suratha holding a tulasī blossom, / speaking of Rāmabhadra with his tongue to his own servants.
The king too, seeing the monkey who bore a charming body, / although knowing him to be Śatrughna's envoy, spoke to the son of Vālin:
Suratha said: / "Lord of monkeys, why have you come here? How are you? / Tell me the entire reason, so that having understood it, I may do it."
Śeṣa said: / To him who was thus speaking, the monkey lord replied, / greatly astonished in his heart at the king who served Rāma:
"Know me, O best of kings, as the son of Vālin, lord of monkeys; / I have been sent by Śatrughna as an envoy to your presence.
My horse has just now been seized by some servants who arrived, / committing a great injustice in haste through ignorance, O king.
Full of joy, go to Śatrughna along with your kingdom and sons, / fall at his feet, and quickly hand over that horse!
Otherwise, with your body torn by iron arrows shot by Śatrughna, / you will lie headless, adorning the surface of the earth.
Where will you go, having stolen the sacrificial horse of him / by whom the lord of Laṅkā was destroyed with ease in an instant?"
Śeṣa said: / To him who was speaking thus and more, the lord of the earth replied: / "You speak all truth; your word is not false.
Yet listen to my word, O servant of the feet of Śatrughna! / I have seized the great horse of wise Rāmacandra.
I will by no means release the horse out of fear of Śatrughna and the others. / If Rāma himself comes and grants me a sight [of him],
then bowing down at his feet, along with my sons, / I shall give my entire kingdom, my family, wealth, grain, and large army.
This is the duty of kṣatriyas, even if it opposes the master: / fighting according to dharma, and moreover wishing for a sight of Rāma.
Conquering those great warriors headed by Śatrughna right now in an instant, / I shall bind them in my house, if Rāma does not come."
Śeṣa said: / Hearing this, the wise Aṅgada then laughed at the king, / and spoke great words filled with immense composure.
Aṅgada said: / "Bereft of sense you speak; this [condition] has come upon you from old age, / that you, foolishly proud of your might, despise King Śatrughna,
who effortlessly slew the demon Lavaṇa, the enemy of Māndhātṛ, / and by whom many powerful and arrogant enemies were defeated in battle;
by whom the rākṣasa Vidyunmālin, mounted on a flying chariot, was slain. / You wish to bind that lord of heroes? You seem to me devoid of intellect!
His nephew Puṣkala is exceedingly mighty and skilled in supreme weapons, / by whom Vīrabhadra, the attendant of Rudra, was well pleased in battle.
How can I describe his valor enhanced by strength, / to whom there is no equal on earth in might, fame, and splendor?
Beside him stands Hanūmat, his mind fixed on the lotus feet of the lord of the Raghus, / whose manifold deeds will surely have been heard by you:
by whom that rākṣasa city on Trikūṭa was burnt down in a moment by force; / by whom Akṣa, the son of the evil-minded king of rākṣasas, was slain;
by whom the mountain named Droṇa, together with its deities, / was brought upon the tip of his tail, again and again, for the revival of the soldiers.
Rāma knows his conduct; no other dull-witted person knows / that lord of monkeys, the servant whom he does not forget in his heart even for a moment.
Lords of monkeys such as Sugrīva, and all the foremost heroes of the earth who are here— / they all serve King Śatrughna, eager to see [the horse].
Kuśadhvaja, Nīlaratna, Riputāpa skilled in great weapons, / Pratāpāgrya, Subāhu, Vimala, and Sumada,
King Vīramaṇi, truthful and a servant of Rāma— / these and other kings, lords of the earth, attend upon him.
In that ocean of heroes, who are you, a mere mosquito? / Knowing this, go to the compassionate Śatrughna together with your sons.
Surrendering the horse, you shall go to Rāma, the lotus-eyed, / and having seen him, make your limbs and whole life fulfilled."
Śeṣa said: / The king said to that messenger who was speaking in manifold ways: / "You point these out quickly; they are all within my sight.
Such strength as I possess, O envoy, even Hanūmat does not have— / he who, keeping Rāma behind him, marched forth in the protection of the sacrifice.
If I, filled with eager devotion, worship Rāma / in thought, word, and deed, then he will soon reveal his own form.
Otherwise, let those heroes led by Hanūmat, endowed with devotion to Rāma, / bind me by force, and swiftly seize the horse!
Go, tell King Śatrughna what I have said: / 'Let the great warriors make ready; I, the mighty one, am marching to the battle.'
Having deliberated, he will do what is proper on the battlefield. / Let them release the great horse, or let them take me."
Śeṣa said: / Hearing this, smiling, the hero went to where the king was. / Having gone, he reported everything just as spoken by Suratha.
